content: A 19-month-old child weighing 12 kg was brought to the hospital emergency room approximately 1.5 hours after reportedly ingesting 7 to 10 ibuprofen tablets (400 mg each). Upon arrival, the child was apneic and cyanotic, responding only to painful stimuli, which were sufficient to induce respiration. Oxygen and parenteral fluids were administered. A greenish-yellow fluid was aspirated from the stomach, but no evidence of ibuprofen was detected. Two hours post-ingestion, the child’s condition appeared stable, though she continued to respond only to painful stimuli and experienced intermittent apnea lasting 5 to 10 seconds. She was admitted to the intensive care unit, where sodium bicarbonate, dextrose, and normal saline infusions were administered. By four hours post-ingestion, the child was easily arousable, able to sit unassisted, and responsive to verbal commands. Approximately 8.5 hours after the accidental ingestion, her ibuprofen plasma concentration was measured at 9 µg/mL. By 12 hours post-ingestion, she appeared to have fully recovered. In two other reported cases involving children weighing approximately 10 kg each, acute accidental ingestion of approximately 120 mg/kg of ibuprofen did not result in any signs of acute intoxication or long-term sequelae. A 19-year-old male who ingested 8,000 mg of ibuprofen over a few hours presented with complaints of dizziness, and nystagmus was observed. Following hospitalization, parenteral hydration, and three days of bed rest, he recovered without any reported long-term complications. In cases of acute ibuprofen overdose, gastric emptying via vomiting or lavage is recommended, although little drug is likely to be recovered if more than one hour has elapsed since ingestion. As ibuprofen is acidic and excreted in the urine, the administration of alkali and induction of diuresis may theoretically be beneficial.
